raw_response:
I would start with **SciDAVis**, then compare **Veusz** and **LabPlot** using one of your normal datasets. **Grace** is another useful option if your work is mainly two-dimensional plots and a Unix/X11-style environment suits you. This ranking reflects fit to your plotting workflow; I did not find comparable evidence establishing which has the most academic users.

## 1. SciDAVis — my first trial for an Origin/SigmaPlot-style workflow

SciDAVis explicitly positions itself in the same application area as Origin and SigmaPlot, with a graphical interface for scientific plotting. Its repository identifies the software as GPL version 2 or later. That makes it a strong first candidate for moving your plotting work to an open-source application. Its project documentation links a manual, tutorials, forums and mailing lists, although I have not measured how quickly those channels answer questions.

Sources: [project description](https://scidavis.sourceforge.net/about/node1.html) and [official source repository](https://github.com/SciDAVis/scidavis).

## 2. Veusz — a focused graphical plotting application

Veusz is designed around producing scientific figures. You build plots from graphical elements and adjust their properties, which is a somewhat different workflow from editing a spreadsheet and selecting a chart. The current documentation lists data import, multiple plot types, error bars and vector output; its repository confirms GPL version 2 or later. A graphical interface is available even though the application also offers scripting.

The project provides a manual, examples, a tutorial, a wiki and a discussion route. I would try it when figure layout and repeatable styling are central to your work, and assess whether its editing model feels comfortable with your own data.

Sources: [overview](https://veusz.github.io/), [current repository](https://github.com/veusz/veusz), and [help resources](https://veusz.github.io/help-support/).

## 3. LabPlot — a broader graphical scientific workspace

LabPlot's official KDE page describes an open-source application that makes plots from spreadsheet data or imported files and exports figures in raster and vector formats. Its homepage describes interactive plotting with a small number of clicks. The project links discussion and support channels through KDE.

Its additional analysis facilities do not conflict with your request: you said that you do not need analysis or modeling, rather than prohibiting software that includes those functions. It deserves a trial if you prefer a data-table-and-plot workflow.

Sources: [application description](https://apps.kde.org/labplot/), [project overview](https://labplot.org/), and [support](https://labplot.org/pages/support/).

## 4. Grace — particularly relevant for 2D plots on Unix-like systems

Grace's official site describes a point-and-click 2D plotting application, with graph customization and export options. Its license link points to the GNU GPL. The site also links a user guide, tutorial, FAQ and forums.

The platform fit needs attention: the official description focuses on Unix/X11 and refers to older Windows ports. Because you did not specify an operating system, I would keep it on the shortlist while checking installation on your actual machine. I am recommending it for 2D scientific plots, with no claim that it reproduces every Surfer or Origin feature.

Sources: [Grace overview and help links](https://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/) and [linked license](https://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/doc/GPL.html).

## Choosing between them

For a useful trial, import a representative dataset, reproduce a figure you already know, adjust its axes and labels, and save/export it. This will expose the practical differences in ease of use and your required plot types. My first two trials would be SciDAVis and Veusz; LabPlot is also a strong direct match.

These recommendations come from project documentation; I have not performed hands-on academic use for this answer. Public help routes are documented, but a reliable popularity ordering and response-rate comparison remain unverified.

**Date qualification:** Your question is dated 26 October 2016. Several opened sources describe later software: SciDAVis's mission page is dated April 2017, Veusz's opened repository describes version 4.2.1, and LabPlot's current pages include 2025–2026 material. An [official July 2016 LabPlot announcement](https://labplot.org/posts/windows-version-of-labplot-is-comming-soon/) describes Windows installers as forthcoming with version 2.3.0 and a Mac port as planned. The current feature and platform lists therefore should not be treated as a verified reconstruction of the exact choices available in October 2016.
